summary: Adds support to the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API) for a flag that tells whether a service is trusted to receive delegated user credentials, based on the Kerberos OK-AS-DELEGATE flag. This lets multi-tier applications avoid handing credentials to untrustworthy servers. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: You wouldn't give your house key to just anyone. This lets a trusted authority mark which helpers may be given your key to act for you.

subtitle: A GSS-API flag that delegates a user's credentials only when central policy says the service can be trusted with them.

tldr.problem: In multi-tier applications a server may use a user's delegated credentials to contact other servers, but handing them to a party that is not trusted enough is a security risk. GSS-API left the delegation decision to the client application, which may not know which services deserve trust.
tldr.mechanism: A new input flag, deleg_policy_req_flag, asks the GSS-API mechanism to delegate only if the mechanism's policy recommends it. For Kerberos that policy is the OK-AS-DELEGATE flag on the service ticket and on every cross realm ticket on the way to it.
tldr.outcome: Clients can delegate if and only if central policy recommends delegation. The old deleg_req_flag keeps its unconditional behavior. The document is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5896 is a Proposed Standard from June 2010 and no RFC listed here obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2743, RFC 2744, RFC 4120 and RFC 4121.

sections.title: The Delegation Problem
sections.content:
Many GSS-API applications work in several tiers. A server takes the user's delegated credentials and acts as the user's agent to contact further servers. Examples in the RFC are web applications that reach e-mail servers or CIFS file servers.

Delegating to a party that is not sufficiently trusted is a security problem. In RFC 2743 the client application alone decides: it sets deleg_req_flag when calling init_sec_context. That forces every client to know which services deserve trust, although a central authority is often better placed to know.
sections.eli5: A helper sometimes needs to act for you. Right now you have to decide on your own whether each helper is safe, even though the school office might know better.

sections.title: The New Flag and Its C Binding
sections.content:
The gss_init_sec_context call gains an input flag, deleg_policy_req_flag, and an output flag, deleg_policy_state. When the input flag is set, delegation SHOULD be performed if central policy recommends it. The output flag is set when policy recommended delegation and delegation was done.

For the C bindings of RFC 2744, one constant stands for both flags, just as GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG maps to two flags: #define GSS_C_DELEG_POLICY_FLAG 32768.
sections.eli5: There is a new box to tick that says "only share my key if the office says it is OK", and a light that tells you what happened.

sections.title: How the Flags Combine
sections.content:
If only deleg_req_flag is set, the mechanism attempts delegation as before. If only deleg_policy_req_flag is set, it attempts delegation only when the mechanism-specific policy recommends it. On success, deleg_state returns TRUE for both the initiator and the acceptor, and deleg_policy_state is set for the initiator.

If the initiator sets both flags, delegation is attempted unconditionally. In that case deleg_policy_state additionally returns TRUE for the initiator only if the policy had recommended delegation.

The policy flag and its state apply to the initiator only. Their state is never sent over the wire.
sections.eli5: If you tick only the old box, you share the key no matter what. If you tick only the new box, you share it only when allowed. If you tick both, you share it anyway, but you also find out whether it was allowed.

sections.title: Kerberos Behavior
sections.content:
When the initiator sets deleg_policy_req_flag without deleg_req_flag, the Kerberos mechanism MUST delegate only if OK-AS-DELEGATE is set in the service ticket, as defined in RFC 4120. Other policy checks MAY be applied. With only deleg_req_flag set, behavior stays as in RFC 2743.

RFC 4120 does not adequately describe OK-AS-DELEGATE across realms, so this document clarifies it. The mechanism MUST examine the flag in the service ticket and in all cross realm tickets in the path from the user's initial ticket-granting-ticket to the service ticket. If any intermediate cross realm TGT lacks the flag, the mechanism MUST NOT delegate credentials.
sections.eli5: For the key to be handed over, every office along the way has to say yes. If even one says no, the key stays in your pocket.

sections.title: Why a New Flag
sections.content:
Strictly, the deleg_req_flag behavior in RFC 2743 could be read the same way as the new flag. In practice a new flag is needed because existing applications and user expectations depend on implementations that do not respect OK-AS-DELEGATE.

The RFC says that in hindsight deleg_req_flag should not have meant unconditional delegation, since promiscuous delegation exposes credentials to hosts the user has no reason to trust. Changing it now would hurt users: some Kerberos implementations do not support the flag in their database, so the KDC would never issue tickets with it set, and users of new client software would never get delegation.
sections.eli5: Changing the old box would break things for people who rely on it. So a new box was added and the old one was left alone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new flag lets the client get help from the KDC in deciding which servers to delegate to. Because it is not communicated over the wire, it creates no new opportunity for spoofing or downgrading policy by itself. Mechanisms should determine delegation policy in a trusted, authenticated way that cannot be spoofed on the network.

The RFC adds that delegating the user's TGT is still too powerful and dangerous. Ideally specific service tickets would be delegated, but that is out of scope. If a client fails to set deleg_policy_req_flag, the worst result is no delegation, which does not expand trust.
sections.eli5: Forgetting to tick the new box just means your key stays home, which is the safer mistake. Handing over the master key is still risky, though.

cells: Only if mechanism policy recommends it
